Good news first: Swiss tenancy law is broadly on your side here. Under Art. 267 of the Code of Obligations (OR), you must return the flat in the condition you received it, **but normal wear and tear is excepted** — and minor scuff marks from furniture are the textbook example of normal wear. The landlord also cannot simply "keep" a deposit: it sits in a blocked account (Kautionskonto) in your name and can only be released with **both** your signature or an enforceable decision. So if you sign nothing, the money is locked — for him too. Here's the path:

## Step 1 — Get your documents in order

- Lease contract (check the deposit clause and any renovation/painting clause — clauses that ignore normal wear are largely invalid under Art. 267(2) OR)
- Move-in protocol from 6 years ago and the **move-out protocol** from last month (this is your most important document — if it notes only minor marks, you're in a strong position)
- Photos, if you have them, from move-in and move-out
- The deposit paperwork (bank, account number) — and check whether it's a **bank deposit or a deposit insurance** (e.g. Swisscaution). If it's insurance, the landlord claims against the insurer, and you should also dispute the claim with them in writing.

## Step 2 — Send the formal letter (below), by registered post

Give him a **10-day deadline** to (a) sign the bank's release form and (b) itemise the alleged damage with evidence. This matters legally: under Art. 257f OR, a landlord who doesn't specify defects within a reasonable time after handover is treated as having accepted the property's condition. A vague "walls are scuffed" claim doesn't survive contact with a demand for specifics.

## Step 3 — If he won't budge, file with the conciliation authority

Rental disputes must go first to the **mietrechtliche Schlichtungsbehörde at the Friedensrichteramt** (City of Zurich). Key facts:

- It's **free of charge** for tenants and you don't need a lawyer
- Forms are on zh.ch / stzh.ch (search "Schlichtungsbehörde Mietrecht")
- Ask for release of CHF 4,500 **plus 5% interest** from the handover date
- Bring your protocols and photos to the hearing. If he can't prove damage beyond normal wear — which is his burden — the authority orders the release, and the bank pays out on that order.
- If conciliation fails, either side can escalate to the Zurich Rental Court (Mietgericht) within 30 days. Realistically, most of these cases settle or get decided at conciliation; expect roughly 2–4 months total.

Even in the worst case, your exposure is small: interior paint is normally assumed to last 5–7 years, so after 6 years it was due for renewal anyway. Courts typically assign the tenant **zero to a small proportionate share** in that situation — not the full deposit.

## ⚠️ One critical warning

If you receive a **Betreibung** (debt enforcement notice — an official form, often yellow/blue) from him, **do not ignore it**. You must file a *Rechtsvorschlag* (objection) within **10 days** or the claim becomes enforceable and the bank can pay him directly. Watch your post carefully.

Also: join or at least call the **Mieterverband Zürich** (mieterverband.ch). Members get free legal representation for exactly this kind of dispute, and they know the local conciliation authority well.

---

## The letter

**Subject: Rental deposit CHF 4,500 – [flat address] – demand for release**

Dear [Mr/Ms name],

I terminated the tenancy for the above flat effective [date]; the handover took place on [date], as documented in the attached handover protocol. I refer to the rental deposit of CHF 4,500 held in a blocked account in my name at [bank, account number/IBAN].

In your [letter/conversation] of [date], you declared that you are retaining the deposit in full due to scuffed walls requiring repainting. I reject this claim for the following reasons:

1. The flat was handed back in the same condition as at the start of the tenancy, apart from ordinary signs of use. Minor scuff marks from furniture are normal wear and tear within the meaning of Art. 267 OR, and their repair is the landlord's cost, not a compensable defect.
2. The paintwork was approximately six years old at handover and had therefore reached the end of its normal life cycle (generally assumed to be 5–7 years). Cosmetic repainting at that point is a landlord expense. To the extent any clause of the lease purports to shift such costs to me regardless of the flat's condition, it is invalid under Art. 267(2) OR.
3. You have provided neither a specific description of the alleged damage compared with the move-in condition, nor any substantiation of the amount claimed. Retaining the entire deposit of CHF 4,500 is in any event grossly disproportionate, even if a defect were established.

I therefore ask you, within **10 days** of receipt of this letter, to:

a) sign and return the enclosed release form so that the deposit of CHF 4,500 plus interest is paid out to my account [IBAN]; and
b) if you maintain your claim, provide me with an itemised statement of the alleged defects — including photos, a comparison with the move-in protocol, and the underlying invoices or quotes.

Should you fail to respond or refuse release, I will file proceedings with the conciliation authority for rental disputes (Schlichtungsbehörde für Mietrecht) at the Friedensrichteramt of the City of Zurich to obtain release of the deposit, with 5% interest from [handover date], and reserve all further rights.

Yours sincerely,

[Name]

*Enclosures: handover protocol (copy), move-in protocol (copy), photos, bank release form*

---

Two notes: send this by **Einschreiben A** (registered post) and keep a copy. And since your landlord is in Zurich, I'd strongly recommend sending it **in German** — it carries more weight and shows you mean business. Say the word and I'll translate it for you, and I'm happy to help you fill in the conciliation form when you get there.

(Standard caveat: I'm not a lawyer and this is general information, not legal advice — but this is a very well-trodden path in Zurich, and the conciliation process exists precisely for disputes like yours at zero cost to you.)

I can give general information about Swiss tenancy law and practical steps, with appropriate caveats that they may want to verify with the official conciliation authority or a tenants' association.

Let me recall what I know about Swiss tenancy law and Zurich specifically:

**Key legal framework:**
- Swiss Code of Obligations (OR) Articles 253–274g govern residential leases.
- Art. 267 OR: tenant must return the property in the condition consistent with the contract, taking into account normal wear and tear ("normale Abnützung" / usure normale).
- Art. 267 Abs. 2 OR: agreements shifting the burden of wear and tear or decoration costs to the tenant in an unreasonable way can be invalid. Specifically, clauses that unreasonably disadvantage the tenant are void ("Die Vereinbarung eines anderen Vertragsinhaltes ist nichtig, wenn sie den Mieter in ungleicher Weise belastet..."). Common "formular" clauses (standard lease terms) that require the tenant to repaint regardless of condition or pay for cosmetic renewal are often invalid if they unreasonably burden the tenant.
- Case law: Swiss Federal Supreme Court has held that normal wear and tear — including scuff marks from furniture, small nail holes for pictures (actually nail holes are generally acceptable), faded paint — is the landlord's cost. Fresh paint has a lifespan; the tenant only bears proportionate costs if the walls genuinely needed repainting and the tenant caused excessive damage. Actually more precisely: the tenant must return the property in the condition received, subject to normal use. The landlord cannot demand repainting merely because the paint is old or the flat looks "lived in."
- Cosmetics vs. damage: distinction between "Schönheitsreparaturen" (cosmetic repairs) and actual damage. Standard clauses requiring repaint on moving out are frequently deemed partially invalid (notable Zurich Obergericht case law; e.g., the requirement to repaint after a certain period regardless of condition has been struck down). The famous rule: clauses obligating the tenant to renovate at their own expense at intervals are invalid to the extent they don't account for wear and tear; but the tenant can be required to return in the agreed condition with normal wear excepted.

**Deposit mechanics:**
- Art. 257e OR: deposit must be held in a separate bank account in the tenant's name ("Mietkautionssparen" / blocked account — "Kautionskonto"). Interest accrues to the tenant. The landlord cannot simply take money from the account; the release requires either tenant's consent (signature of both parties on the release form) or an enforceable court decision/enforcement order.
- So the landlord "keeping" the deposit typically means he refuses to sign the release form at the bank. Without the tenant's signature, the bank won't release funds to landlord; without landlord's signature, tenant can't get money back. Deadlock resolved via courts.
- Important deadline: Art. 257f OR — the landlord must notify the tenant of defects/damage within a reasonable time after return of the property; if the landlord fails to do so, the landlord waives the right to assert claims (this is the "Verwirkung" — implied waiver). Case law: "reasonable time" is usually around 30 days (some say up to a month; a Swiss Federal Court decision suggested about one month for notifying of defects after handover). Actually let me be careful: BGE 132 III 733? I recall the general principle that the landlord must claim within a "angemessene Frist" — commonly cited as one month. The handover protocol (Übergabeprotokoll) matters hugely.

**Formal step: conciliation authority (Schlichtungsbehörde / Schlichtungsamt für Mietrecht):**
- In Zurich, disputes about deposit return are "Mietrechtliche Streitigkeiten" that must go through the Justice of the Peace / conciliation authority for rental matters: "Friedensrichteramt" — in Zurich city it's the "Friedensrichteramt der Stadt Zürich" with the mietrechtliche Schlichtungsbehörde. Filing is free of charge (no court fees) for tenants in rental matters — yes, proceedings before the conciliation authority in tenancy matters are free for the tenant (no court costs). You don't need a lawyer. You can obtain an order ("Verfügung") or a settlement.
- Deadline: the claim for deposit release prescribes... the tenant's claim for return of deposit: 5 years? The landlord's claims against tenant: Art. 257f. For the tenant, claims prescribe after 5 years (Art. 127 OR / 128). But there's a critical procedural point: to prevent the release of the deposit to the tenant, if the landlord wants to assert claims, they must notify within reasonable time, and to actually block, they should file with conciliation. If tenant applies to conciliation and landlord doesn't assert counterclaims timely, deposit must be released.
- A key practical lever: The tenant can request the conciliation authority to order release of the deposit. If the landlord doesn't appear or doesn't establish claims, the authority orders release, which the bank accepts as enforceable title.

**Handover protocol:**
- The move-out inspection and protocol is central evidence. If the user signed a handover protocol noting only "normal wear" or listing scuffs, that matters. If no defects recorded, landlord is largely out of luck. Also the move-in protocol from 6 years ago matters — if walls were already used/scuffed at move-in.

**Paint lifespan:**
- Courts and standards (e.g., SIA norms) assume interior paint has a useful life of roughly 5–7 years (some say 5–8). After 6 years of tenancy, the paint was near the end of its normal life cycle; wear proportionate to a nearly exhausted paint life is normal wear. Many decisions hold that a tenant is not liable at all for cosmetic condition after paint has reached its normal lifespan; at most the tenant owes a proportionate share if they caused damage beyond normal use.

**Practical steps to advise:**

1. Gather documents: lease contract (check deposit clause and any renovation clause), move-in protocol, move-out protocol, photos (move-in, move-out), the deposit account documents (Kautionsversicherung or bank guarantee? If it's a bank deposit, get the account details, bank, account number, the deposit certificate), correspondence with landlord, and the landlord's written justification.
2. Ask the landlord in writing for an itemized justification: what exactly, cost basis, quotes/invoices. Set a deadline (e.g., 10–14 days) and explicitly request he sign the release form for the deposit account. Send by registered mail (Einschreiben) — or at least keep proof.
3. Check whether it's a bank deposit (blocked account) vs. deposit insurance (Kautionversicherung e.g., Swisscaution, Kautionsgarantie). If insurance, the landlord makes a claim against insurer and tenant gets billed — different route but same substantive fight.
4. If no satisfactory response, file with the conciliation authority for rental disputes — in the City of Zurich: Friedensrichteramt Stadt Zürich, mietrechtliche Abteilung (Stadthausquai 17, 8001 Zürich — I should double check; the mietrechtliche Schlichtungsbehörde of the City of Zurich is at Stadthausquai 17). Free of charge, no lawyer needed; forms available online (zh.ch / stzh.ch). Request: release/order to pay of CHF 4,500 plus interest, possibly plus CHF 150 or so in costs? Tenant can claim interest at statutory default rate (5%).
5. At the hearing, bring evidence. Conciliation is mandatory before court for rental disputes.
6. If unresolved at conciliation, either party can escalate to the Mietgericht (Rental Court) of the Canton of Zurich by filing within 30 days of receiving the conciliation outcome ("Rechtsöffnung"? no—"Klage" after "Beweisverfahren" maybe). Note the two-step: conciliation decision + 30 days to file action.

Also mention: the landlord cannot just keep the deposit; the money sits in the blocked account until release by both signatures or enforceable decision. If the user simply signs nothing, the money is safe but inaccessible; the conciliation route unlocks it.

Also: deadline pressure — Art. 257f: landlord must assert defects within reasonable time (case law: about one month). Since move-out was last month, the landlord did communicate within that window (he says walls scuffed), so that argument may not fully apply, but if he's vague, ask for specifics; if he misses deadlines or gives no specifics, argue waiver. Also note: even if he notifies, he must prove damage beyond normal wear AND that the flat was returned in worse condition than received (per protocols).

Also: re-painting cost apportionment: even in cases where tenant is liable, courts often reduce by the age of the paint. After 6 years, with paint life ~5-7 years, tenant share ≈ 0–15%. So a full 4,500 CHF for repainting a Zurich flat (how big? 4,500 is a typical deposit for a ~3.5–4.5 room flat) is disproportionate; repainting might cost 2,000–4,000 CHF, and the tenant share would be near nil unless damage is real.
